copies.headline: John's Depth Buries Noah's Top-Heavy Bet
copies.body:
Noah is putting the whole season on Achane and Cook doing something absurd, and honestly they might. That backfield duo projects for 33 combined, seven points clear of anything John can run out there, and if Achane hits his ceiling in Miami's opener this whole preview reads differently by Sunday night. The problem is everywhere else. Garrett Wilson is a legit WR1 but the receiver room falls off fast after that, Colston Loveland is a rookie tight end asked to be a difference-maker, and Drake Maye capping out at 16 isn't winning any shootouts.
John just has more good football players. Puka Nacua alone outscores Noah's best three receivers by himself some weeks, Brock Bowers gives him a tight end that would start over Loveland on either roster, and he's got Stafford throwing to Nacua while Caleb Williams sits as a 17-point luxury on the bench. The Jaguars defense and Cam Little are boring, sure, but boring wins Week 1s when the other side needs everything to break perfectly. Noah needs Achane to go nuclear and everyone else to overperform. John just needs Tuesday-morning-obvious lineup decisions to hold.

copies.headline: Chase Against the Field, Literally
copies.body:
Isaac's whole season-opening pitch is Ja'Marr Chase plus depth nobody else has, and it's a legitimate argument. Malik Nabers and Terry McLaurin as your WR3-adjacent options is absurd, and even with Chase soaking up targets this group projects six points clear of Kaleb's receivers. The problem is everywhere else. Javonte Williams and Cam Skattebo are touchdown-dependent committee backs, Bo Nix is a fine but capped floor at QB, and Hockenson-or-Kincaid at tight end is a rounding error either way.
Kaleb built this roster top-heavy in the right direction. Ashton Jeanty and Breece Hall give him the best backfield in the matchup by seven points on paper, Justin Herbert is the best quarterback either team runs out, and Harold Fannin gives him a real tight end instead of a coin flip. Drake London and Ladd McConkey are plenty behind Chase's group without being an actual weakness. The projections have Kaleb up two, which feels about right — Isaac needs Chase to go nuclear and one of his shaky backs to hit a score just to survive the floor Kaleb's roster provides everywhere else.

copies.headline: Grant's Receivers Try To Outrun Burrow
copies.body:
Grant opens the season leaning on the best wideout room either roster brings to the table. Amon-Ra St. Brown at 19 is the single best player in this game, and the depth behind him is absurd for a Week 1 lineup — Zay Flowers, Waddle, Christian Watson and Godwin all projecting double digits means CJ's corners are getting cooked from multiple angles. Dallas Goedert gives Grant a mild edge at tight end too, and Omarion Hampton anchors a backfield that's deeper than it looks once you get to Jadarian Price and Pollard.
CJ's counter is simple: Joe Burrow is the best quarterback on the field by two points, and Jonathan Taylor matches Hampton play for play at running back. The problem is everything after that. Rashee Rice and Egbuka cap out CJ's receiver corps at solid-not-scary, and Jake Ferguson is a real downgrade at tight end. This projects as a track meet Grant should win by playing volume — more places for points to come from beats one great quarterback in Week 1.

copies.headline: Hurts and Barkley Give Rezac the Edge
copies.body:
Adam opens his title defense against a Logan roster built like a mini Eagles reunion, and that's the whole problem. Jalen Hurts projects for 21, Saquon Barkley another 18, and that duo alone outproduces Adam's best guys at both spots combined. Adam counters with Jayden Daniels and a Kenneth Walker/Bucky Irving committee that's fine but unspectacular, the kind of RB room that needs garbage-time work to hit its number. Where Adam claws back is the perimeter — Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Chris Olave give him two legit spike weeks, and Sam LaPorta at tight end is a quiet two-point edge over Isaiah Likely.
It's close on paper, about eight points by best-lineup math, but Logan's floor is just higher. Jeremiyah Love gives him a second bell-cow behind Barkley, and Justin Jefferson anchors a receiver room deep enough that Tetairoa McMillan and Michael Pittman are afterthoughts rather than needs. Adam's margin for error is thin: if either QB or a receiver underperforms, there's not much juice behind Rome Odunze and Jalen Coker to bail him out. Logan should win this one running away from the RB and QB spots alone.

copies.headline: Christian's Top-Heavy WRs Face Peter's Bijan Insurance
copies.body:
Peter has the best player in the building at two spots — Lamar Jackson gives him a two-point edge at quarterback and Bijan Robinson is the kind of workhorse who makes an RB2 conversation irrelevant. But that's also his ceiling. Drop past Bijan and Peter is running Jonathon Brooks or Jordan Mason in a timeshare nobody trusts yet, and his receiver room is deep but capped, with Pickens, A.J. Brown and Tee Higgins projecting like solid WR2s rather than the guy who wins you the week.
Christian's the mirror image. Trevor Lawrence and Jordan Love won't scare anyone, but CeeDee Lamb and DeVonta Smith give him two legitimate spike weeks at receiver, and Chase Brown plus Travis Etienne is enough juice at running back to hang with Bijan-plus-committee. The swing spot is tight end, where Chig Okonkwo projects for 7 against Tucker Kraft's 10 — a gap that could decide this by itself. Math says Christian by two, but Bijan alone can erase that before halftime.

copies.headline: Gibbs and Depth Have Mitchell's Number
copies.body:
Leif opens the season with the flashier top of the roster and none of the connective tissue. Josh Allen gives him a real ceiling at QB, and McCaffrey-Henry is a two-headed monster if both stay healthy, which is doing a lot of work in that sentence. But look past the names and it thins out fast — Woody Marks and Kaelon Black as your RB depth, Caleb Douglas as your fifth receiver, Jason Myers as a top-10 asset on this roster. Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jayden Reed need to actually hit rookie-year and sophomore-leap upside for this to work, not just flash it.
Mitchell's roster doesn't have a marquee name at the top so much as it has quality at every single slot. Jahmyr Gibbs is a true bell cow with receiving work baked in, Nico Collins is a legit WR1, and Tyler Warren gives him a real receiving tight end instead of touchdown-or-bust guesswork. Even his QB2, Daniel Jones, would start on half the teams in this league. The projections have this close, but Mitchell's floor is a lot higher than Leif's, and in Week 1, with nobody's lineup locked and injuries lurking everywhere, floor wins.

intro: Isaac-Kaleb is the closest thing on the board to a real fight, two points separating them with both rosters looking legitimately stacked, so start there if you only watch one game. Everybody else has a lean: John's got Noah by ten, Logan's shoving Adam around by eight, and Christian looks like the first guy in the league to open 0-1 by a laugher. Standings don't matter yet, but nobody wants to be the team explaining a sub-111 output in week one.
